transcript: It all started in Mar del Plata.
At 17 I built my first product: a games website, which changed my life. I'm self-taught: I read a lot and study online.
2021 – 2022 · TACH Argentina: a digital wallet, end to end. Remote: the back office, the landing page and the app, on web and mobile.
2023 – 2024 · Ada ITW: teaching people to code. JavaScript and React: projects, hello worlds and students starting from zero.
2024 · Tsoft, on Tuenti: gamification you can measure. The roulette and the referrals; then a dashboard to measure referrals, recurrence and gamification. (Illustration with fictional data.)
2026 · CompliA, the RAG assistant of Telefónica's compliance portal: artificial intelligence in internal production. I designed and built it. (Demo clip, with sample data.)
Also at Tsoft: Supernova Eventos, an events micro-app (prototype, with fictional data), and raising the team's level: I trained colleagues.

And a path of my own: Eclipse (in development), HandyX (in development · launches Nov 10), Volta (demo), Velmar (demo made for a client), DentalOS (demo), games-market (test bench) and Kinetic Studio (32 trailers in code). All of it, in code.
Every path opened since I was 17. It all grows into the same thing: seeking new challenges.
New challenges are what drive me: boosting businesses and automating hard processes. I'm not afraid of any industry: startups, corporates, agriculture, space, mining, oil & gas.

Technologies, by where I used them. At work: React, TypeScript, Next.js, React Native, Tailwind, Node.js, SQL, CI/CD and RAG with an LLM. In my projects: security (HttpOnly cookies, CSRF, 2FA, Argon2), Python, C, motion with GSAP and WebGL, and tests with Vitest and Playwright. Studying: machine learning fundamentals, AWS and Azure.

An agentic system, split into parts: 11 agents with separate roles. Not a prompt: a system with roles. Specification first, code second; every claim carries its level of evidence; gates with human approval; tested, not eyeballed.
Run of 10/27/2026, all green: Eclipse-Web 463 tests, Eclipse backend 779, internal portal 132 and 14 browser journeys.
Ignacio Gauna, from Mar del Plata, Argentina. I build AI software that ships.
Open to new challenges: startups, corporates, agriculture, space, mining, oil & gas. ignaciogauna.developer@gmail.com · linkedin.com/in/ignacio-emanuel-gauna

method.label: Method
method.title: How I create value.
method.lead: Six steps. Each with something I did, not a nice phrase.

steps.name: Understand the problem
steps.text: Before building, I understand the context and the business. Talking to the people who use the software changes what gets prioritised.
steps.example: In-person day with clients in Buenos Aires (April 2026): demos, alignment and direct conversation about their real challenges.

steps.name: Align and negotiate priorities
steps.text: I agree on scope and priorities before writing code, and I hold the difficult conversations when they're needed.
steps.example: At Tsoft I take part in technical decisions with the team and support people who join.

steps.name: Design
steps.text: I design the interface and the system together: rules, states and limits before pretty screens.
steps.example: Volta and DentalOS: navigable demos with their own identity and labelled data.

steps.name: Build in stages
steps.text: I split the work into small batches, each with its acceptance criteria.
steps.example: Eclipse moves forward in documented batches, with approval gates.

steps.name: Show and validate
steps.text: I show something that works as early as possible and test it: automated tests, visual QA and demos.
steps.example: Velmar: a navigable demo for a client, with sample data.

steps.name: Deliver and learn
steps.text: I ship with CI/CD, document what I learned and apply it again.
steps.example: At Tsoft I work with deployment pipelines, integrations and CI/CD on Telefónica and Tuenti projects.

method.cycle: A loop, not a line: what I learn when delivering comes back in as the next problem.
method.readsMore: See the models and how I apply them

system.label: System
system.title: An agentic system, split into parts.
system.lead: I code with agents, but each one has its own part and nothing ships without a person who approves.

points.title: Not a prompt: a system with roles
points.text: I built 11 agents with separate responsibilities (product, UX/UI, design, marketing, and frontend, backend, cybersecurity, games and trailer architects), with skills that load depending on the task.

points.title: Specification first, code second
points.text: Every change starts with a short document: problem, scope, acceptance criteria and how to roll back. The work is cut into small batches.

points.title: Every claim carries its level of evidence
points.text: I tell apart what I read, what I tested locally and what runs in a real environment. What I haven't tested is labelled «not tested».

points.title: Gates with human approval
points.text: The agents don't publish, spend or change prices on their own. I authorise publishing and spending.

points.title: Tested, not eyeballed
points.text: The main projects have automated tests, end-to-end tests with Playwright and CI that runs the tests and the build. Run of 10/27/2026, all green: Eclipse-Web 463 tests, Eclipse backend 779 and internal portal 132, plus 14 complete browser journeys.

points.title: Visual QA with binary criteria
points.text: Redesigns are compared against the previous state at several widths and with reduced motion. I state the limits: I test in Chromium.

points.title: Cost and honesty as design rules
points.text: No invented testimonials or clients, everything fictional says «Demo», and no new dependency or spending without my OK.

system.limits: What I don't say: that the agents work on their own, that the system has been audited or that a pentest has been done. The backend's database tests run in CI; I did not run them in the run above.

business.metaTitle: How I think about business — Ignacio Gauna
business.metaDescription: The models from The Lean Startup, The Mom Test and Blue Ocean Strategy that I use, and where I applied them: HandyX and Eclipse.
business.label: Business
business.title: How I think about business.
business.lead: Three books that changed how I build. From each, the models I use most and where I applied them in my projects.
business.note: The examples come from my projects. Where there is no data, I say so; I don't make up metrics.
business.reading: Reading now: SPIN Selling, by Neil Rackham, on consultative selling.

lean.title: The Lean Startup
lean.idea: A new product is an experiment. What you build matters less than what you learn, and the speed that counts is the speed of each loop.

models.d: The core loop: turn an idea into a product, measure how people respond and learn whether to keep going or change. You plan it backwards: what I want to learn, what I need to measure, and only then what to build.
Two assumptions hold everything up: value (does it help anyone?) and growth (how does it reach more people?). Test the riskiest one first.
The smallest version that completes one full loop. Not a half-built product: an experiment with a goal.
With what you learned, decide: stay the course, or change one piece of the strategy without throwing away the rest.
Measure what changes a decision, not what looks good. And ship in small batches so mistakes are cheap and early.

loop.caption: The Build · Measure · Learn loop: what matters is how long each loop takes.

fork.caption: Pivot or persevere: what you learned picks the branch.

apply.d: Before building the app, a landing page with a waiting list and specialist pre-registration. Its only goal is real pre-registrations: the first experiment on the value hypothesis.
The public counter only appears from 20 sign-ups and rounds down. I'd rather show a small, honest number than an inflated one.
Every change is a batch with its spec, its acceptance criteria and an approval gate. A mistake costs one batch, not a project.
The site shows demos of the business working before proposing anything: the shortest way to learn whether it interests whoever is looking.

mom.title: The Mom Test
mom.idea: How to talk to customers without them lying to you, even out of kindness: ask your mom whether your idea is good and she'll say yes.

models.d: Talk about their life, not your idea. Ask about specifics in the past, not opinions or the future. Talk less and listen more.
Compliments, generic claims («always», «would use», «would pay») and feature requests without the why. When they show up, go back to specifics.
A conversation is worth what the other person puts on the line: time, reputation or money. If it ends with no next step, it didn't advance.

items.bad: Would you use an app to get more jobs?
items.good: How did you get your last three jobs?

items.bad: Would you like to see the price before confirming?
items.good: What happened the last time you were charged something you didn't expect?

items.bad: Do you think it's a good idea?
items.good: What did you try to solve this, and why did you stop?

swap.caption: Example questions for a specialist or a resident. They illustrate the rule; they are not a real survey.

steps.d: «What a great idea.» Commits to nothing.
A second meeting, a trial with a date.
An introduction to someone else or to the decision-maker.
A deposit, a pre-sale, a payment.

apply.d: In the internal portal an unanswered attempt doesn't change the state: only a real conversation moves it forward, and a specialist is «committed» only once a start date is agreed.
In April 2026 I travelled to Buenos Aires for an in-person day with clients: demos, alignment and direct conversation about their real challenges.

blue.kicker: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne · 2005
blue.title: Blue Ocean Strategy
blue.idea: Instead of fighting over the same market (the red ocean), create a space where the competition stops mattering (the blue ocean).

models.d: Raise value for the buyer and lower cost at the same time, by changing the factors the industry competes on.
The factors an industry competes on and each offer's value curve. A different curve is a different strategy.
Eliminate, reduce, raise and create: the grid that forces you to stop copying the competition.
First buyer utility, then an accessible price, then cost, and finally adoption.

errc.title: The four actions, applied to HandyX

eliminate: Surprise charges: nothing extra without your OK.
Handing out your phone number: it isn't shared.
reduce: Calling people one by one for quotes: proposals arrive in one place.
raise: Price clarity: labour, materials and fee, itemised.
Knowing where the job stands: live tracking.
create: The specialist sets their price, with a suggested reference.
Extras that are proposed and accepted in the chat.

errc.caption: Taken from what HandyX's landing page and demo already show.

canvas.title: A strategy canvas, qualitatively
canvas.caption: A qualitative reading to think through the strategy; not measured data. «The usual way»: asking around or finding an ad.

apply.d: Instead of competing only on the number of specialists, HandyX competes on certainty: see the price first, nothing extra without your OK, and your phone stays private.
Instead of promising in a meeting, Eclipse's site shows the business working and puts price, scope and maintenance in plain sight.
